The committee of supply is not set up until the debate on the speech from the throne has been disposed of.

I am astonished at this proposition coming from the Minister of Finance, who is so well informed, not only about the experience of this house over the

Advance Payments to Grain Producers years but also the fact that time and time again where new programs are introduced involving cost sharing responsibility with respect to something that includes provincial participation, we do it without any estimate but with a bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are getting away from the point entirely; it is a question of estimates.
We want a bill.
It is a question of the rights of parliament.
My, how you have changed since those brave days of 1956.

As I pointed out, the Prime Minister said it would be an affront to parliament if, in advance of its assembly, he indicated to the banks they could, as in other past similar emergencies, start paying out funds to these needy farmers and then subsequently the banks would get from parliament, in legislative form, the necessary guarantees. The Prime Minister says he could not give that, but he has given an i.o.u. in the same form without consulting parliament and bypassing parliament in connection with this major expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is untrue, and you must realize that.
It is not untrue in any shape or form. My. hon. friend has a great habit of calling black white and vice versa.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I call that untrue right now.

My hon. friend will have an opportunity to speak and explain the proposition, but he simply cannot answer that. We have from time immemorial, when introducing a new shared responsibility program, put it in legislative form. I refer to such things as unemployment assistance, old age assistance, and so on. All of those propositions in which a new principle is involved are introduced in this house by legislation, and it is that which provides the government with the authority to make the agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are fine people to be talking about that now.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: May I have leave, before the leader of the C.C.F. party speaks, to ask the hon. member a question? Am I right in assuming, where there is a statute dealing with a certain matter, that the Prime Minister should make a pledge to the premier of Saskatchewan-
What statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: -that he will take certain action in contravention of that statute, without calling parliament?
I am saying the Prime Minister has done exactly that without a statute. He has given an i.o.u. to the provinces upon which they apparently are relying because machinery has been set up-
Before it has been introduced.

-for these payments. I am not objecting to that. I am saying an emergency existed and probably some proposition to the provinces was necessary. What I say is that now parliament has assembled, at the first opportunity parliament should be asked to ratify the proposition of the Prime Minister. Surely, the Prime Minister has enough regard for parliament that he would want the opinion of the parliamentarians assembled here with respect to this proposition.

There is room to take objection to the method that the government is following in introducing these two measures without introducing the companion measure that would provide the farmer with some cash. What the government is really doing, particularly under the legislation that provides for guarantees on bank loans, is to say to the farmers of the west who are in this emergency, we will ask the unanimous consent of the House of Commons to interrupt its procedures so that you can get a mortgage, so that you can incur a debt from the bank, but we will not ask parliament to interrupt its procedures in order that money be made available to pay you cash for the grain under the snow.
One would wonder whether the government by this operation, without the companion operation, is interested in putting the farmers more deeply in debt, getting them further obligated to the banks of this country. I would hope that the government will ask the members of the house to take this emergency action. As a matter of fact, and I do next think this would be breaking a confidence-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Is the hon. member opposed to the bank loans?
Is that not a bright remark, Mr. Chairman? I did not expect to be able to get ahead of my hon. friend.
Answer the question.

However, I thought that I would be able to get this point across, namely that we should like to have been asked to deal with all three measures, particularly the one that is of the greatest benefit, instead of being asked to deal with only two measures.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Would you
answer my question?

We are very much in favour of this legislation. I was about to say, Mr. Chairman-and I do not think this would be breaking a confidence; if it is, I will apologize-but I was asked by the government whip whether I or our group would have any objection to following the procedure of interrupting the debate on the speech from the throne so that we might deal with legislation having to do with the emergency grain position in western Canada. My immediate reply was that I was sure we would be pleased to follow this procedure. The hon. gentleman did not spell out to me exactly what was involved and I therefore assumed that the government was going to ask parliament to set aside the debate on the speech from the throne so that we could take the appropriate steps to make the money available to the farmers, namely the $3 per acre payment. Hence, instead of being opposed to anything that has been going on, as the implication has been made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, we have been most happy to co-operate in every way to see that this legislation is passed through parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: It did not sound like it.

The Minister of Finance takes
a rather strange position. His is a procedural opposition to giving some money to the western farmers at this time. I think it is not only an important practice but the most important practice of parliament, namely that parliament is the master of its own procedure and that while there are important practices and procedures, these can be interrupted or can be modified with the unanimous consent of the house. Instead of raising this procedural objection in order to withhold money that is badly needed at this time I suggest that the Minister of Finance, through the leader of the house, should ask the house for unanimous consent to proceed with the other measure at this time so that the farmers will have a chance to get the money they so badly need. I ask the minister from Saskatchewan whether he would not support this procedure by parliament so that the money might be made available at this time.
When the resolution was being introduced the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he did not think that at this particular stage of the debate very much discussion would be needed and that the main discussion could take place on the bill. I am rather sceptical of statements by ministers of the crown with regard to the value of debate on the resolution preceding a measure that
Advance Payments to Grain Producers is to come before this house. I consider the debate on the resolution stage of a money bill is an exceedingly important part of our deliberations. There is here afforded the opportunity for members to bring forward their objections to legislation, their criticism or their suggestions for improvements in time for the government to consider important changes to the bill before it is in fact introduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I judge that the hon. member, from my earlier remarks on the importance of the resolution stage, did not draw the inference that when I was in opposition I discussed this point at great length and reached the conclusion, from a study of historical documents and rule books, that the resolution stage is not as important as are other stages of the bill. Just because I happen to be a minister of the crown now I am not suggesting any curtailment of debate. My opinion was based on my survey of the situation years ago when I was on the other side of the house.

That is an even more disturbing statement than the original one, particularly in view of the statement that has been made by the Prime Minister dumping the whole question of procedure and changes in the rules in this house in another debate. I want to warn the government that they will be in serious difficulty if any effort is made by the government to have its majority override the minority group or groups in this house in order to bring about a change in the rules that will curtail the necessary opportunity for discussion by members of parliament and by members of the minority groups.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no such suggestion as that, and the hon. member knows it.
I am not too sure. I have watched this government in operation for some time. I remember when they were on this side of the house how strongly they obj ected to legislation-
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. What has this to do with the resolution?

Mr. Chairman, I think this has an extremely important bearing on the resolution that is before us. I am discussing the procedure of the house in bringing forth this resolution and there has been substantial discussion on this very point this afternoon.
I was about to say, Mr. Chairman, that when hon. members opposite were on this

Advance Payments to Grain Producers side of the house they took the greatest exception possible to the government's legislating by an item in the estimates. I think it would have been preferable, not only to have brought in the matter of payments for grain under the snow at this time but to have done so by legislation in the proper and regular manner.
As to the problem itself on the prairies, may I say that this is not a problem that has occurred this year only. It is a problem we have had in various degrees in other years in the past. No one knows just how serious the problem may finally be until we know whether or not and to what extent the grain now under the snow can be salvaged in the spring. A few years ago when a much larger percentage of the crop went through the winter, spring conditions were exceptional and a very high percentage-almost 100 per cent-of the grain was recovered in the spring, and it was very often in better condition than the grain that was harvested in the fall before the snow came.
I was not aware of the figures until the minister made them public to us of the great progress in harvesting that had taken place during the month of November. There is one thing of which western farmers are capable, namely using their machinery and their know-how, in spite of adverse conditions, in order to do things that are almost miraculous. We now know that there is approximately 15 per cent or 16 per cent of the grain under the snow as far as the western crop is concerned. We would hope that of this 15 per cent a very substantial part may still be recovered when spring arrives.
We are being asked to pass a resolution which will precede a bill to provide provisional payments for unthreshed grain in the prairie provinces. I take it that this legislation is to be temporary, and I ask the minister that question. I take it this legislation is to be for this year only, and that if another situation like this should arise next year, then presumably it will be necessary for parliament to introduce a similar bill and go through the same type of discussion.
I am very anxious at all times that emergency legislation should not be made permanent legislation, but I do feel that the government should consider whether or not it would be possible to amend the cash advance legislation so that the wheat board and its officers may be entitled to make money available when grain is unthreshed and under the snow.
After all, in making this money available a great deal of protection is given to the Canadian wheat board, because they take possession of the farmer's permit book, and if the


farmer is to stay in the business of producing grain, even if he should find it difficult, he nevertheless has to repay, as he will, the loan when he delivers grain to the elevator. I would think that this kind of legislation is valuable legislation. Although there are only a few years where a large or substantial percentage of the grain is under the snow, nevertheless for certain individual farmers it does occur rather frequently. Therefore, instead of asking parliament to deal with this situation every few years, the Canadian wheat board, under the cash advance act, could have the right to make these kind of advances.
The legislation to provide guaranteed bank loans, the payment of $3 an acre, is necessary. But all of this legislation applies to prairie producers who can qualify for payment, and it provides very limited sums of money, or allows them to borrow very limited sums of money. I think the government should know why there is such pressure from western Canada for legislation of this kind when 15 per cent or 16 per cent of the grain is under the snow. Why are thousands of farmers who are adversely affected by the weather putting so much pressure on the government to get payments that are very small payments, and guarantees on rather small sums of money, as far as an individual is concerned?
The fact of the matter is that a large part of the grain producers of western Canada find it extremely difficult to keep on their farming operations and to stay in business. If the farmers of western Canada were engaged in a prosperous occupation, if they were engaged in an occupation in which during an ordinary year they could make a reasonable net income, they would not have to demand the kind of emergency legislation with so much strength as they are now doing.
There is other action that the government could take. I would like to see the government act by paying deficiency payments, as a result of the requests which have been made by farm organizations. If the government would make the deficiency payments available to farmers, as the farmers have requested, then there would be much less need, if any need at all, for guaranteed bank loans on which the farmer will have to pay a very substantial interest charge. I am hopeful that the government will come to a decision on this matter soon, and will meet the price-cost squeeze which is the great economic problem facing the farmers of western Canada.
As far as the legislation to provide bank loans is concerned, and as far as the action taken by the federal government to meet the emergency by paying some monies out of the federal treasury is concerned, the government is responding to requests which have

oeen made oy all of the farm organizations in western Canada, in addition to requests which have been made by three provincial governments. As I understand the negotiations which have gone on so far, the Social Credit government of the province of Alberta, the C.C.F. government of the province of Saskatchewan and the Conservative government of the province of Manitoba have asked the federal government to consider the situation a national emergency and to pay from the national treasury monies to farmers with grain under the snow. They asked the government to accept this as a national emergency.
Instead, in spite of the unanimous request of these three provincial governments, governments of different political complexions, the federal government has refused to consider a national emergency by paying the full cost of the payments for grain under the snow. Indeed, the government is asking provincial governments to pay half of the cost, which means, in many instances, that they are asking the very people who will get assistance to pay through their taxes to the provincial government a substantial part of the assistance that they are about to receive.
There is other action which could be taken in this regard. I believe provincial governments have been acting by providing payments to farmers in order to assist them in moving fodder for livestock, in the moving of seed grain, to provide a work and wages program, and to undertake other expenditures within the jurisdiction of provincial governments. They have asked the federal government to accept its responsibility in this field by considering the situation a national emergency.
Mr. Chairman, we are, of course, quite prepared to support the legislation, and we shall, but I think the minister might give consideration to my suggestion that changes could be made in the cash advance legislation so as to empower the wheat board to make advances on grain which is unthreshed so that it would not be necessary to come to parliament on repeated occasions to get the kind of legislation we are now being asked to pass. The government is taking some action; but I think in view of the request which has been made by the spokesman for the Liberal party in this house and the request that I have now made the government should consider a further interruption in this debate, or an extension of this interruption in the throne speech debate so that we can take action to provide the emergency payments in cash to the farmers who are in difficult circumstances at this time.
Advance Payments to Grain Producers

Mr. Chairman, the opposition, as is not unusual, appears to be in a very considerably confused state of mind in regard to this resolution and the other proposals which have been made by this government in order to relieve the situation caused by the early snow in western Canada.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, in dealing with the matter, mixed up several things which are actually quite separate. When the Prime Minister announced, in the latter part of September, the assistance that this government would be prepared to provide to farmers who had their crops under the snow, there were four distinct things-
Does the hon. minister mean the latter part of November?
Yes. Did I say "September"?
Yes.
It was November 27.

Thank you. There were four things that were mentioned. First, there was something which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River mentioned, namely that P.F.A.A. payments would be speeded up as far as possible; second, that a bill would be introduced as soon as parliament assembled to provide for government-guaranteed bank loans on unthreshed grain and, third, that a form of cash advances, or what we are calling in this bill provisional payments, would be made as far as unthreshed grain is concerned.
He simply said he would give it consideration.

Fourth, we made an offer to provide a certain amount of assistance to farmers who had 50 per cent or more of their grain unthreshed. Each one of these provisions stands on its own feet, and any attempt to mix them together and combine them in one measure naturally causes confusion; a confusion which flows, I suspect, from the confusion which exists in the minds of the hon. gentleman and his friends opposite.

I asked the
minister a question with regard to the companion bill which is not now before the committee. Am I correct in saying that the provinces, under that, are paying out money to the farmers?

If the hon. member will hear me out I think he will get the answer to his question. There has, of course, been full information given in connection with these matters; that information was made available a considerable length of time ago,
96	HOUSE OF
Advance Payments to Grain Producers and the farmers in western Canada are certainly not labouring under the misapprehensions which hon. members opposite seem to share.
The remarks of the hon. member from Kenora-Rainy River were extremely contradictory. He said, to begin with, that we were very slow in making an announcement regarding the assistance we intended to give to these farmers whose crops had been snowed in, but a little later he said it was an affront to parliament that we should be doing anything in the matter. In other words, he completely contradicted himself in the space of two or three minutes.
I said no such thing. I said the' government had not taken advantage of the first opportunity to acquaint parliament of what the scheme was-a scheme involving financial contributions.

Hansard will show what the hon. member said. He went on at considerable length to say that it was an affront to parliament that we had provided for a form of assistance on the basis of $3 an acre without consulting parliament. Then, only shortly afterwards, he was saying that we were very slow in making any announcement in connection with this matter at all. Then the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River expressed great surprise when these two resolutions came on the order paper that there was nothing in them in connection with the $3 an acre payment. I do not know why he should have expressed any such surprise, because I distributed copies of the bills as requested by the Leader of the Opposition on Friday afternoon. The hon. member telephoned me afterwards to ask me about this matter, and said "I suppose you are going to introduce that in the form of an estimate?" and I said "Yes". Yet he stands up in the committee today and makes a great to-do as though he were terrifically surprised that the resolution should appear on the order paper without any mention of the $3.

I said that after parliament had adjourned for the weekend, to my surprise I found there was nothing which referred to the arrangement with the provinces on this matter which is of such great public interest, and I asked the minister how, legislatively, he proposed to deal with this, and he said, "By estimate". I say that is the wrong procedure.

Anyway, all this surprise on the part of the hon. member is so much eye-wash. The hon. member talked about it being an affront to parliament that the $3 an acre payment should be dealt with by an estimate, and the hon. member for Assiniboia


followed up his remarks to some extent though his complaints were on a somewhat different line. I will deal with that presently.
At the moment I should like to point out to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and to the committee as a whole that this is the manner in which these national disasters, with regard to which the dominion government has taken some responsibility for providing assistance along with the provinces, have been dealt with in the past. When the Winnipeg flood occurred, when the Rimouski fire occurred and when the Fraser river floods occurred they were dealt with in each case by means of an estimate, and we are dealing with this disaster in exactly the same way. As a matter of fact, it is, I think, the only reasonable way of dealing with a situation of this kind when it arises while parliament is not in session; you cannot wait for several months until parliament assembles in order to pass an act to deal with these events.
Parliament is now in session. Give us the act.

You have to make an
arrangement with the provinces as to what share the dominion government is to bear and what share they are to bear, and get a scheme into operation. That is exactly what was done in this case.
I should like to put a question on that point. Is this to be an estimate in the final supplementary estimates of this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not the finals.

It will be in the first supplementary estimates which it is possible for us to bring in at this session.
The hon. member for Assiniboia made a great point that farmers are being denied payments because, he said, we are refusing to bring in a bill to provide for this $3 an acre payment at this time. He went on to say that procedural objections are being raised by the Minister of Finance which will cause money to be withheld from the farmers. He accused us of being unwilling to interrupt the ordinary course of parliament in order to make a contribution to these farmers while being willing to interrupt it in order to make them a loan. As a matter of fact, the cash advances we intend to provide in these provisional payments are not loans; they are cash advances which in this case we are calling provisional payments so that there may be no confusion. These are not loans. The farmers pay no interest on them and, therefore, the statement which the hon. member for Assiniboia made is not correct.

The whole point is this: in order that the farmers may be able to take advantage of these provisional payments and of the guaranteed bank loans as soon as possible it is necessary for us to put legislation through parliament because there is no legislation which covers the situation at present. All these statements about farmers being denied these payments and about delays in connection with these payments of $3 an acre are completely inaccurate. The farmers are getting these payments in each of the three prairie provinces at the present time. The schemes are being administered by the provincial governments. The provincial governments are putting this money out right at the present time. There is no delay as far as any farmer is concerned because an act has not yet been passed.
Is federal money being paid without an estimate being passed?

Each provincial government is administering its own scheme. It is making these payments. When it has made the payments it will call on the dominion government to pay 50 per cent of the amount paid out, but that time has not yet come and, therefore, we shall have plenty of time-
After the money has been spent.
-to have this matter dealt with by parliament and covered by an estimate which will be before us fairly shortly.
Shocking.

The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate says "shocking". But this is exactly the way in which the government of which he was a member dealt with the Winnipeg flood, the Fraser river flood, the Rimouski fire and any other disasters in connection with which they gave assistance. And yet the hon. member now says it is shocking.
Would the minister permit a question? Would he inform the committee what would happen if this estimate were not passed?
Have the election this year instead of next year.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member knows quite well what would happen in that event. The government would resign. In the meantime, of course, the provinces would have been responsible for the whole amount. They would have paid it out. But the provinces, of course, have confidence in this government. Unlike the Leader of the 79951-0-7
Advance Payments to Grain Producers Opposition they feel quite confident that they will secure a share of the $3 an acre payments that have been made.
Those are the only points I feel I should deal with at this time. I regret to say that there has been a great deal of argument this afternoon which is completely out of order on this particular resolution but in view of the fact that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and the hon. member for As-siniboia raised the question of the $3 an acre payment and confused it with the issue before the committee I thought I should make it clear to the committee exacly what the situation is and clear up any misapprehension and misunderstanding that may exist in regard to the matter.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure one would experience great difficulty in attempting to find at any time in the history of this parliament a more disturbing
statement of the responsibilities of a government to parliament than the statement we have just heard from the Minister of Agriculture. The only extenuating circumstance in this case is that as one who has devoted his activities prior to coming into this house to matters other than the law the hon. gentleman could not possibly be expected to have the same appreciation of constitutional practice that one certainly looks for in both the case of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce from Manitoba who sometimes acts as though he were the minister for Canada.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and others who have spoken in this debate, recognizing the plight of farmers in western Canada, have recognized the desirability of bringing forward and considering at this time legislation which is said to be of an emergent character to deal with an actual economic situation that confronts the farmers of western Canada. I am sure both of them would likewise have said, if the point had immediately confronted them, that such legislation should not be confined only to the farmers in one section of Canada but should also apply to farmers throughout the country who are faced with situations that are comparably serious to the one that provokes this particular legislation foreshadowed in this resolution.
By that I mean that the farmers in all parts of Canada are greatly concerned about the difficulties that arise as a result of acts of God. The farmers of one section of Canada covered by the bills envisaged in these resolutions have experienced a situation that also from time to time confronts farmers in my own section of the country. The beet growers of southwestern Ontario, as some hon. members know, have had their crops under the

Advance Payments to Grain Producers snow and have experienced great difficulty but there is nothing in this legislation, in so far as the statements of the ministers who have spoken thus far are concerned, to indicate that farmers in southwestern Ontario or anywhere else in Canada are going to be given the opportunities provided for in the two resolutions that are before us or in the resolution which should be before us soon with regard to the federal-provincial co-operative arrangement; but we will have an opportunity when we discuss these two bills to bring forward desired points of application to districts in Canada other than those in western Canada, districts which we all recognize require perhaps even stronger assistance than is provided for in the bills to follow the resolutions before us.
But what is the situation with regard to the measure about which the Prime Minister spoke so strongly in the statement he made on November 27 last? As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River stated, the Prime Minister announced various programs that the government had in mind for assistance. There were, as the Minister of Agriculture just said, the P.F.A.A. payments which the Prime Minister said may be made-he did not say would be made but may be made-as soon as possible. He said the government had decided to bring forward guarantees on bank loans for unthreshed grains but he did not say, as the Minister of Agriculture has just observed, that the government would bring in amendments to the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act of 1957.
What the Prime Minister said on that occasion was that the government was giving consideration to an amendment to the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act of 1957. He emphasized in Winnipeg and in one other city in western Canada-I believe it was Saskatoon -that the government was going to bring forward without delay a measure in which the provinces would be invited to co-operate to deal with crops under the snow.
And pay half the cost.

And pay half the cost, as my friend the hon. member for As-siniboia reminds me.
The Minister of Agriculture said we had no need to be surprised by the failure of the government to present to parliament at this time the third measure. The speech from the throne indicated that we had the right to expect that the measure to which the Prime Minister attached such importance would be presented to parliament in proper legislative form consistent with the practices of this and other similar parliaments in the


commonwealth of nations. These are the words to be found in the speech from the throne:
The severe, unseasonal snow in the prairie provinces interrupted the harvest rendering necessary emergency legislation which will he considered at the earliest possible opportunity.
If we did not have the right and the justification to believe that the legislation that was going to be presented at this time was that referred to by the Prime Minister in the language I shall now place on the record, then I think hon. gentlemen have not carefully read the speech from the throne or have not recalled the implications of what the Prime Minister said on November 27 last. Let us hear what the Prime Minister said on that day:
While it is hoped that a large proportion of the crops now under the snow will be salvaged in the spring, a considerable amount of loss is inevitable. Therefore, in order to provide some compensation to the farmers who have suffered misfortune-
Listen to these words:
-the dominion government offers to share on a 50-50 basis with each of the three prairie provinces in an assistance scheme of the following nature-
Then he went on to outline the scheme in these words:
(a)	A payment of up to $3 an acre on a maximum of 200 acres per farmer, on unthreshed crops of wheat, oats, barley, rye, and flax. The federal government would be prepared to regard as eligible for this assistance any individual farmer who has been prevented by snow conditions from harvesting 50 per cent or more of his field crops.
(b)	For specialized crops, such as sugar beets, potatoes, vegetables, sunflowers, etc., assistance up to a maximum of $600 per individual farmer, provided that snow conditions have prevented him from harvesting 50 per cent or more of the crop.
That is what they tell the press, but not parliament.

That is what they told the press. That last statement serves to justify the merits of the observation I made that this particular kind of measure should apply not just to one section but to all sections of agriculture in Canada, particularly when one realizes the extension by reference to the various kinds of agricultural products that are included under this federal-provincial arrangement.
I tell the committee that in my judgment the reason why we are not dealing with the bill in regard to this particular measure is that the Minister of Finance is anxious in his budget to give the impression that he has transformed the country from a deficit into a surplus position. Because of his anxiety to present a balanced budget he has decided to defer this matter until the budget has been delivered and until all matters having to do with the budget have been completed in this house so as to reduce the amount

of the financial obligations that he as Minister of Finance will have to meet. He wants to be able to say-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is not a
tittle of truth in what you are saying.

He wants to do with regard to this measure exactly what he did with regard to unemployment insurance benefits. Last year he brought in his budget with no reference to unemployment insurance taxes, and when the budget was passed-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Order.
-we were confronted with an additional $78 million in taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Order.

What the minister is now doing with regard to this measure he is doing by way of an estimate. The Minister of Finance is trained and has an understanding of the meaning of the rights and obligations of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is trained to recognize the hon. member's pretences.

But he is prepared to ignore parliament in order to achieve a certain purpose, to relieve himself of the embarrassment which has attended him in the matter of deficits ever since he assumed the office of Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: False in every word.

Why should not this be brought to parliament? Imagine the Prime Minister of Canada, a man who talks about parliament, and has talked about it as no one in the history of this country has, going out to western Canada and saying, "I will not consult parliament, I will undertake to see that my government pays 50 per cent of the cost of this measure," a measure which in principle all members recognize as necessary in order to meet the plight of the farmer at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order-
A plight which has been greatly contributed to by hon. gentlemen opposite.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member has put into the mouth of the Prime Minister words that he did not utter. The Prime Minister never said, "I will not consult parliament." I hope the hon. member will withdraw that statement.

My hon. friend is right, he did not say, "I will not consult parliament", but what I am saying, and what 79951-0-7J
Advance Payments to Grain Producers the Minister of Trade and Commerce fails to understand, is that the Prime Minister, without having first come to parliament, made a commitment which first of all should have been made in this parliament and resolved in this parliament. Even Mr. Bennett-
We should not have done anything for the farmer.
No, that is not so.
My hon. friend has great knowledge of constitutional practice.

We recognize that something should be done for the farmer. We say that the government should take the earliest opportunity, because of the practices of parliament, to bring forward a bill on which parliament could express approval of this measure at the quickest moment.
Parliament was not in session.

Of course parliament was not in session, but that is all the more reason why the government should take the earliest opportunity to deal with this. The Minister of Agriculture says that moneys are now being paid out by the provinces. That, of course, is necessary; but does the hon. member not realize that what the provinces are now doing is paying out money, 50 per cent of which they are responsible for and 50 per cent of which the government and this parliament are now morally responsible for as a result of the act of the Prime Minister committing this parliament and this government without first having come here and asked parliament to approve of this measure. That is what we are complaining about. We are complaining about the use by this government, or the abuse by this government, of the rights and of the privileges of parliament, and particularly by one who is now going to bring in a bill of rights to safeguard human rights as well as to safeguard the rights of parliament. I say, furthermore, that this particular-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would you say that if the Prime Minister were in the house? He is not here at the moment.
I would say it if the Prime Minister were here and he ought to be here.
Why is he not here?

In so far as the
public is concerned the Prime Minister is the one who is responsible for proposing this measure. I would tell the Prime Minister that if he were now sitting in his seat.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
You are very courageous in
his absence.

Private Bills
Bring in the Prime Minister. I will withhold what I am going to say until he comes. I would tell the Prime Minister what I now tell the Minister of Finance.
You are jealous because the farmers of eastern Canada are not getting the chance to get something.

My hon. friend is right. I would like to see the eastern farmers get the benefit of this kind of legislation. T am sure the member for Middlesex West, the member for Elgin and all this galaxy of Tories from southwestern Ontario would join with me in saying that this kind of legislation should apply to the farmers of southwestern Ontario as well as to the farmers of other parts of Canada.
You have no snow down there.
My hon. friend says we have no snow down there. What this government has done in failing to recognize-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but it being five o'clock, it is my duty to leave the chair-
Mr. Chairman, would you not think, since the occasion is unique and the Prime Minister has now come in, that the rules ought to he violated at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is your idea, violate the rules.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Under standing order 15 I have to leave the chair to permit the house to proceed to the consideration of private and public bills.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It being five o'clock the house will now proceed to the consideration of public bills, pursuant to standing order 15.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the house would consent to revert to committee and proceed with the debate that was taking place at five o'clock. I think there is a general understanding that that would be the case.

I might say something on that point. We in this group are in agreement with that procedure, not that we like to see the rules of the house set aside but because it is our understanding that the bills have not been printed, as yet. Since it is a long standing custom that we should not be asked to debate or consider legislation that is not in printed form and we cannot see, therefore we are agreeable to revert to the business that was interrupted.
We are also agreeable, sir.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: On both counts, I think the matter can be arranged. Standing order 74 says that before second reading all bills shall be printed in the English and French languages. I regret to inform the house that none of the public bills has yet been printed in French and very few of them have been printed in English, and it would therefore be incompetent, under the rules, for the house to proceed with public bills, since they are not ready for second reading. There are no private bills. The house will revert to the business which was interrupted at five o'clock.
Mr. Speaker, I was invited by the minister-
Wait until we get into committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Don't be so
impetuous.
Try to keep a little decorum.
It is very difficult.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Churchill-Mr. Flynn in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the making of provisional payments to the producers for the 1959-60 crop year in respect of unthreshed grain in the designated area, as defined in the Canadian Wheat Board Act; and to provide for the costs, expenses and other financial obligations required in the making of such advances; such measure to include such further related and consequential provisions as are necessary to give effect to the foregoing.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the course of my remarks the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that I would not repeat, in the presence of the Prime Minister, what I had said about him in relation to the failure of the government to present to parliament in the proper traditional and constitutional manner, the measure that provides for assistance on a 50-50 basis to farmers in western Canada whose crops are under the snow. The Prime Minister is now in his seat and I welcome the opportunity of saying in his presence what I had said in the presence of less distinguished ministers, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture. Although they are distinguished, they are not as distinguished.
What I had said was this: We all welcome the opportunity of passing at the earliest

Advance Payments to Grain Producers
opportunity farm legislation of an emergent character that would give relief to the farmers of western Canada, particularly when we consider that much of the need for this relief was occasioned by the policies of this very administration. I said also that while it was right that the two particular pieces of legislation should be before parliament we had all of us, with justification, having in mind the reference in the speech from the throne, concluded that the government was going to bring forward in parliament at the earliest opportunity the legislation, not an estimate, authorizing the payment of the federal share of this federal-provincial arrangement to assist farmers whose crops were under snow. I said that I thought it was execrable that the man who is now head of the government of this country, who has gone up and down the length and breadth of this land over the years talking about the rights of parliament, talking about civil liberties, the man who shortly is going to introduce in this parliament a bill of rights, should be the head of a government that would have committed this parliament without any authorization from this parliament for deserved assistance to farmers of western Canada under this federal-provincial arrangement.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: What about the provincial governments?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Never mind; I am now dealing with the statement concerning the responsibility of the Prime Minister in this matter. I will deal with that one after. I am now dealing with the dare of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that I should say before this great champion of human rights what I said in his absence.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: You are warming up again; that is fine.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: I say this, that the Prime Minister of Canada cannot possibly justify committing this parliament until this parliament itself has been committed to any expenditure of public money. The precedent for this will be found in all kinds of measures, not only under Liberal but under other Conservative governments. Even the government of Mr. Bennett, the government of the blank cheque, got authority for the blank cheque by way of authorized legislation from this house. But not this Prime Minister. We are going to assist a particular group of people; we are going to commit ourselves with the three western provinces, whether or not parliament has given us any authority so to do.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Do you object?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
My hon. friend says, do I object? Of course I do not object to giving assistance. What I do object to is, for one man, even though he may be the Prime Minister, acting when parliament is not in session as though he were himself the very embodiment of this free institution.
Now, I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce is satisfied that I have repeated in the presence of the Prime Minister what I said in his absence.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: May I have the opportunity of replying, if that represents the entire statement because I came in for the purpose of hearing this statement.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister wish to speak on this particular point?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Would the Prime Minister mind if I just completed this point? What I wanted to point out was that the Minister of Agriculture said that what the Prime Minister was doing with this measure had been done by previous administrations on other issues; that is undoubtedly what the Prime Minister has in mind. I thought, therefore, I would anticipate him and correct him before he falls into any grave error. In the case of Rimouski, in the case of the Manitoba floods, and in the case of the floods in British Columbia, it will be found that the government of the day made an announcement not outside parliament but while parliament was in session. My hon. friend need not look surprised. He was here at the time. I know he said something in connection with the Manitoba flood. The then prime minister did not go out and make a speech outside of parliament saying to the provinces, we are going to pay a percentage of the amount of money you give to assist the people who require relief. The prime minister in all those cases did what the Prime Minister of Canada in this instance should have done.
What the Prime Minister should have done,
I say with great respect and confidence, was to say to the three western provinces, parliament is not sitting but my government will recommend to parliament a proposal along these lines. If the Prime Minister had taken that course; if he had come in here and said to parliament, I have told the provinces that the government is prepared to give assistance to the farmers of Canada whose crops are under the snow on a 50-50 basis and I am sure the house will recognize the desirability of acting at once on this matter, then I believe the bill would have passed within an hour.

Advance Payments to Grain Producers

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Not if you had been talking.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: My hon. friend says, not if I had been talking. Unless there is some reason that is not now apparent, I think it would have passed. In any event, as my colleague says, that does not affect the principle of this thing. I do not want the Prime Minister, in following me, to say that as a result of what I have said it is apparent that the members of the opposition are against this kind of measure. I know the debating tactics of the Prime Minister very well.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: He knows yours, too.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
If you understand mine, then you will show greater condescension and knowledge than is apparent at the present time. Let me say to the Prime Minister at this time that we are in favour of this kind of measure. We would like the correspondence with the provinces to see whether or not the financial arrangements made by the Prime Minister are sufficient; whether they really meet the needs. We would like to have all the facts so that we can judge whether or not this measure is adequate.
With regard to the two other measures, bills for which have been supplied, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River said, we are in favour of such measures. The Prime Minister, who is now going to reply to the constitutional, to the legal aspect, I hope will not fail to recognize that he has acted contrary to one who upholds the traditions of parliament. He sought, by his own commitment and that of his government, to assume a responsibility which belongs to parliament alone. If there is one thing of which this assembly is jealous, it is its right to vote public moneys. The Prime Minister has failed, in these circumstances, to recognize that right and no amount of debating contortion will be able to alter the situation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: I always enjoy hearing the hon. gentleman speak. Sometimes he generates more steam than is safe for him and he proceeds to enlarge and expand in that expansive manner of his-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Pompous manner.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Why not?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
No. In his expansive
manner he proceeds to build up a very good case. As a matter of fact, as I listened to him, it so happens that I was glancing over a book on parliament I had in my room. I am not going to say that there is any applicability at all. It is entitled "Orders of the Day, Memories of Nearly Fifty Years of the House

of Commons" by the Right Hon. Earl Winter-ton, P.C. I do not know whether or not the hon. gentleman has read it. It is most helpful in understanding the traditions of parliament and in maintaining those things which will be maintained so long as this government is in power, namely the supremacy of parliament. I can understand the degree of his exuberance when he looks back on the record of the government of which he was a member in that famous debate known as the pipe line debate in which he and other members of the government at that time learned the meaning of constitutional and parliamentary government. I should like to read from this book at page 16 as follows:
During the debate on the address, a new Liberal M.P.-Mr. Herbert Paul, the historian-in a maiden speech made a ferocious, though somewhat confused, attack upon the Conservative party.
I simply pause to point out-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: The similarity.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: -that the hon. gentleman has just spoken in a somewhat similar manner. The quotation continues:

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
who held high office after the first world war, followed with his maiden speech. He made one of the neatest retorts X have heard in the Commons. "The honourable member's speech", he said, "reminded me very forcibly of a passage in the Bible, 'Paul, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning hath made thee mad'".
As I listened-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Remember the words of St. John.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: I will welcome any quotations that are applicable to the matter in question. However, I point out this circumstance. At all times it has been made clear that this matter would be brought before parliament. At no time was there any suggestion whatsoever that parliament should be by-passed. What was made abundantly clear was this. The general plan would be worked out with the provinces to present to parliament and at the earliest possible date the legislation and the particular estimate would be made available to parliament. That has been done as definitely and as clearly as the constitution will permit and also as the exigencies of the moment in western Canada require.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister permit a question?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
In his absence the Minister of Agriculture has indicated that payments are actually being made in all the provinces. Does the Prime Minister suggest that this matter has not been worked out?

Advance Payments to Grain Producers

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Will the right hon. gentleman refer to one thing that I said that would be disparaging of the personality of Mr. Bennett?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: The blank cheque.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Of course Mr. Bennett was guilty of the blank cheque. Mr. Bennett on occasion was as guilty of dictatorship as is the Prime Minister.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: I am not going into that matter. I think the hon. gentleman will recall no one who was as friendly to him as was that distinguished prime minister.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
He does not deserve to have disparagement cast on him so frequently as has been the case on the part of the hon. gentleman. I make that point clear.
I simply rose to say this, Mr. Chairman. We endeavoured to bring about at the earliest possible date the introduction of measures to benefit the western farmers in their circumstances. We discussed with the various provinces the plan which we would submit. That plan is before them. If it is not in keeping with the wishes of parliament, then all that hon. gentlemen opposite have to do is vote against it in order to say that the benefits to the farmers shall not be paid.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: That is not before parliament.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Oh, I realize that. Talk about mental manipulation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Who is doing that?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
realizes this. We followed the normal course, the necessary course. We had in mind the kind of legislation and the plan we would place before parliament to the end that unnecessary delays would not take place in the administration. The plans were placed before the various provinces. As I said on that occasion, the government has decided
to submit to parliament a measure, and then I set out the measure. Then I went on to say that the government is giving consideration to the amendment to the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act of 1957. Then following in the next paragraph there is reference to the plan which we intend to present through the medium of an estimate at the earliest possible date.
The course of action that has been followed on many occasions in the past is one which is in keeping with the traditions of parliament and which assures each and every member the opportunity to stand up and be counted. An opportunity is certainly going to be given to the hon. gentleman to vote either for or against the assistance which we have in mind to place before parliament through the medium of an estimate. He will then be able to carry his criticism to that limit that comes to all of us, namely to stand up and say, "I am opposed to this measure"-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: I am in favour of it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
-rather than indulge in a dialectical discussion about imaginary unfairness done to parliament.
I conclude there and remind the hon. gentleman once more of the facts, and also those associated with him on the front bench, including the hon. gentleman who is about to rise in his place, namely the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who will give us a dissertation on parliament which will not be in accordance with the views he expressed at the time of the pipe line debate.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
I realize, Mr. Chairman,
that, the Prime Minister having made my speech for me, it is rather redundant for me to rise and attempt to make it myself. The Prime Minister began his brief-happily brief-intervention in this debate and ended it with two typical Diefenbaker tactics, with diversions. He read a totally irrelevant passage from the author called "Old Lace", by Mr. Churchill on one famous occasion, and ended by trying to anticipate what I had to say. But what the Prime Minister completely ignored throughout the whole of his speech was that the Minister of Agriculture told us that money is now being paid out of the treasuries of three provinces of this country, half of which the Prime Minister has given an undertaking that he will ask this parliament to reimburse.
Mr. Chairman, I take no objection to that at all, and neither does anybody on this side of the house. We recognize that there was an emergency last November. We recognize that it was perfectly proper for the Prime Minister to go to Winnipeg and make this
[	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Advance Payments to Grain Producers
offer, as the head of a government with a large majority, and say: "I will introduce this into parliament and ask parliament to vote it". I do not think the Prime Minister was as scrupulous in his use of language as his predecessor was; but he is not in any respect as scrupulous in his use of language as his predecessor, and perhaps it would be pedantic to object on that ground. We are not objecting at all to what was done in November. We are not objecting at all to the proposal which was made in November, and I think on this occasion I speak for the whole of the opposition on this side of the house. What we are objecting to is the fact that money is being paid before parliament, being in session, has the chance to say anything about it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Paid by whom? By the provincial governments.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
The Minister of Agriculture told us that this scheme was already in operation and money was being paid out by the provincial governments. It is not being paid out by the federal treasury.
It is true, as the Prime Minister said, that if a majority of this parliament voted against that payment, it could not be made; but no one anticipates that that will be so. However, I would remind the Prime Minister, as my colleague for Essex East has already done, that it is the preservation of forms, as the Prime Minister told us on many occasions much more eloquently than I, which must be preserved, and it is the preservation of the forms of parliament which is just as important as the substance if we are going to continue to have a free government. If the Prime Minister does not believe that, why does he suggest we should consider matters like the bill of rights?
The plain fact of the matter is that if what the Minister of Agriculture says is true, as I assume it is, and money is being paid out, it is because an agreement has already been reached with these provinces. Therefore there is no reason on earth why a bill should not have been brought in. This excuse that it has to be an estimate, is of course, the most palpable excuse. It would be much better done by a bill, although I have never objected to legislation by estimates.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Did the government to which he belonged ever pass a bill to deal with a disaster such as this; or with other types of disaster to which the dominion government gave assistance? Did his government ever pass a bill on any single occasion?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: The government to which I belonged never passed bills; in our day parliament passed them, and that is exactly the point I am making.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: What about the pipe line?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: And the use of closure?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister talks about the pipe line. At least we brought the bill in. We did not ignore parliament altogether as he has done here.
If I can answer the Minister of Agriculture, there was a crisis two or three years ago when we were in office over a very great surplus of grain, and my right hon. friend, Mr. Howe, who was sitting on the government side at that time, did not simply tell the wheat board that the government would pay the carrying charges on the considerable surplus. He brought in the legislation and gave parliament a chance to express its voice first, and that is what should have been done in this case. It is the most ridiculous thing we have yet been asked to do, to pass these two bills, which are only a supplement to the main measure. They are bills which will probably cost the treasury a good deal less than $1 million in all, if they cost anything.
The Minister of Finance, who above all is the minister who should protect the rights of parliament to vote the money he spends as the trustee of parliament, is saying: "We will go on and let someone else spend the money we have promised, and in our good time we will bring you in the bill after the expenditure has been incurred". The fact that we insist on the proper forms of parliament being carried out is no excuse for the cheap, backbench jibes which were made when the hon. member for Essex East was speaking about our opposition to this measure. We are not opposed to the measure. We want the measure here so that we can vote for it, but parliament is being ignored and bypassed, although some time later we will be asked to put our rubber stamp on it. I do not care how big the government majority is; that is not the right way to treat parliament, and that is what we are objecting to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, these words come ill from the hon. gentleman. What happened on an earlier occasion will not be forgotten by those who sat in this house in 1956. The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate was a very vocal member of the administration of that time. On that occasion what happened was this. It was proposed in the fall of the year to ask the banks of this country to lend money to western producers without there being any legislation at all on the statute books for the purpose. A letter was written by the minister of finance

Advance Payments to Grain Producers
ot the day to the banks, in which he said: "It you will advance this money to the producers; we will introduce a bill in parliament to make it good".
Now, this hon. member who has just spoken was a member of the administration at that time which embarked upon that course. Parliament was not in session; the minister of finance simply wrote a letter to the banks and asked them to lend money. There was no statutory authority for it whatever. Then they said: "Oh well, we will get parliament to come along and provide that later".
It will be well remembered by those who sat in the house on January 27, 1956 when the minister of trade and commerce of that day rose in the house to move the resolution anticipating the introduction of the bill for the purpose. This is what he said, as reported at page 605 of Hansard:
It seems to me that there should not be a prolonged debate on this legislation. The provisions of the bill have been in effect since November 15.
That was the date of the letter.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have made reference to the precedents in connection with relief for farmers, and that is one I had in mind because I had read the debate. I had taken no objection whatsoever to the government making a commitment in the emergency such as they have done. What the minister of trade and commerce at that time did, and what I say this government should do, was, at the first opportunity, to present to parliament the recommendation that they promised a partner they would present. What has been done here is that some form of guarantee and undertaking has been given to the provinces, and while we are asked to deal with supplementary or companion forms of legislation for the same emergency, we are not given the opportunity to put in legislation form at the first opportunity the type of relief for which the Prime Minister has given an undertaking to the provinces. That is what I suggest should be done at this time.
There seems to be some confusion. I think this has just been an oversight. I think the government was intending to put this through in the form of an estimate, but it is suggested that that is not the best way of dealing with something that is related to two other pieces of legislation which are put before us at this time, and I hope the government will reconsider this matter.
Surely, there would be no difficulty about getting ready in legislative form the outline of the willingness, as expressed by the Prime Minister, to share with the provinces 79951-0-8
in the cost of certain forms of relief in the present emergency. That could be done while we were discussing these other bills. The maximum terms are all outlined in the statement which the Prime Minister made to the press. There is nothing there which could not be put into the form of a statute, and this could be done within a couple of days while we were debating the two companion bills. However, this is what I fail to understand: the Minister of Agriculture says that payments are being made-I think he said this-in all the provinces. That is contrary to the information I have.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: I said that payments were being made, I thought, in all the provinces. But certainly they are being made in some of them.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
The minister put it in such a form that one would imagine they were being paid in all the provinces, and I intend to rise at the first opportunity and ask him to verify his statement, because I read a few days ago in Winnipeg papers that the minister of agriculture of Manitoba, at least, had stated that his province was not in a position to produce cheques in payment to the producers until some time well advanced in February. I therefore think that some verification is desirable with regard to the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture.
I still say that this is basic to a consideration of the other two measures. We are to have this legislation this week, and I have already suggested the form in which it should be presented to the house. The reason is this. The bill which will be founded on the resolution presented by the Minister of Trade and Commerce is, as hon. members will be aware, confined to the ambit of the products within the jurisdiction of the wheat board act. The proposition made to the provinces for cost sharing in connection with certain assistance is much wider than that. There is no reason, with respect to this legislation, to restrict the type of aid either to the western provinces or to certain kinds of producers in the western provinces. If these arrangements were incorporated in the bill we should have the opportunity right now to decide whether or not vegetable growers and others, who apparently are included in the commitments to the provinces but who are not referred to in either of the pieces of legislation, should, in other parts of the country, get similar consideration. But that opportunity for discussion and for advice to be given to the government is denied to parliament at this stage.

Advance Payments to Grain Producers

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I, also, would like to congratulate you upon your appointment to your very important office. It is one, which, I know, you will handle justly and well.
While sitting here during the debate this afternoon my mind rambled back on several occasions, to my constituency and when I heard hon. gentlemen opposite speak, some of whom I thought got a long way from the matter which we are discussing, I wished some of them had been in my riding and seen the condition of the snowed-under crops. Possibly, then, they would have understood more clearly the nature of the bill which is before the committee this afternoon.
I feel I should say a few words about this bill, representing as I do, the constituency of Meadow Lake, a riding which was hard hit by the very unseasonable harvest weather. Many areas in my riding had the heaviest rainfall on record during the time when we usually expect harvest weather, only to be followed by 20 inches of wet snow in many parts of the constituency. A further snow storm followed.
This bill will help many farmers who are not qualified for a payment of $3 an acre up to a maximum of 200 acres owing to the fact that in some areas they have more than 50 per cent of their crop harvested. A large percentage of the crop which was threshed was damp and farmers received a very low grade.
I want to compliment the Minister of Transport on the very rapid action he took to make it possible to move tough and damp grain to the terminals for drying. Inspections under P.F.A.A. have had to be held up in many areas on account of the very low acreage harvested. Further inspections will have to be carried out in the spring when the harvest has been completed. I think many townships will qualify for assistance under the P.F.A.A., where crops were neither swathed nor stooked. The grain was standing when the storm hit, but was left lying flat on the ground. I think this bill is very urgent, and I certainly hope it will be passed without undue delay.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my first words will be to congratulate you for having been appointed to the office of vice chairman of this house. We know that your impartiality will be appreciated by all and that wisdom will guide your every decision.
Mr. Chairman, after listening to hon. members this afternoon, I realized that I did not 
know much about parliamentary procedure, because I thought that when money bills were introduced, custom demanded that they be subject to the approval of parliament. As a matter of fact, I found that the discussion and also the way the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made his suggestions on November 27th last, had nothing in common with parliamentary procedure.
Indeed, in a press release of September 27, he had intimated that he would hasten the payment of funds distributed under the P.F.A.A. He said he would introduce a bill providing guaranteed bank loans. He also talked about interim payments for grain crops that have been covered by snow. At that time, he also stated that he would grant the farmers a 50 per cent compensation for their crops.
Last Friday, the Prime Minister stated in this house, that it would be appropriate to introduce with the least possible delay, two bills: one dealing with cash advances on unthreshed grain and the other concerning bank loans guaranteed by the government. This legislation, we admit, is known to be urgent, and we shall raise no objection to the Prime Minister asking that those bills be dealt with today. However, we are suprised not to see any bill regarding the Prime Minister's suggestion to the effect that the federal government pay 50 per cent of losses sustained by farmers whereas 50 per cent would be carried by the provincial governments.
Finally the purpose of the bills before us is to compensate farmers whose grain has remained under the snow. The situation is indeed pretty bad, since producers did not have the advantage of benefiting from the amounts which the sale of their grain would have brought in last fall. Those producers invested the cost of seeding and other work carried out during the year, and we can easily understand their plight.
We have witnessed various disasters in western Canada which were caused by bad weather conditions, and this reminds me of the year 1931, when I was staying as a trainee on a western farm in order to round out my practical knowledge of agriculture. That year, Saskatchewan had been particularly hit by a drought, such as the west had not yet known. The grain producers did not even try to harvest their crops. I remember the panic which seized the west at the time, when those farmers had lost all the fruit of their labour and could not count on any assistance from the government of the day which, of course, was then at a

dead end, economically speaking, as it is the case today, because there was also a Conservative government at the helm.
In those days, I realized that our western farmers were having a hard time. Today's state of affairs presents a certain similarity with conditions prevailing that year. And people have again to deal with a Conservative government.
Now I remember the remarks of some hon. members last year, and again, two years ago- and I refer now to one of the eight C.C.F. leaders sitting in this house-since each one of them has his own personal political ideology-and that is the hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. Argue) who intimated that I was not familiar with the problems facing western farmers, when he stated in his province that I was a funeral director. Well, I must say that, while I fully respect that profession-whose services the hon. member for Assiniboia as well as the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) will some day appreciate-the hon. member for Assiniboia made false statements about me, to increase his political capital, when he claimed that he was the only expert in this house on farm matters.
Mr. Chairman, I have the greatest liking for western farmers, and I have had occasion to know them. However, I must say that I have no less liking for eastern farmers. For two years in a row, disasters have completely ruined the crops in certain areas of that part of the country. In fact, in 1958, the crops were completely destroyed by hail, and the following year there was a flood, whose consequences were no less serious. Yet, no assistance was then given to those farmers by the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, I wish that when our ministers introduce legislation to protect western farmers they would display the same spirit when it comes to hardships also affecting eastern farmers.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, we shall vote in favour of the resolution. I will say to the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner), who in the course of his unfortunate remarks a moment ago stated that we were opposed to legislation in favour of western farmers, that we will support the resolution and that we are not jealous of western farmers.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
