Mr. Chairman, this afternoon we witnessed a typical day in the House of Commons, the C.C.F. running in one direction and the Liberals in the other. The hon.
79951-0-8J
Advance Payments to Grain Producers member for Assiniboia started off by telling us that this was a measure by which the prairie farmers affected by the adverse conditions would not get payments. The hon. member for Assiniboia who I am sure is a close follower of The Western Producer should have read the January 14 issue of that publication. In bold print on that day it carried this headline: "Farm Payments Near $1 Million".
The article goes on to state:
Payments totalling nearly $1 million for Saskatchewan farmers who were unable to thresh their crops have been approved by the plant industry branch of the department of agriculture, it was announced by agriculture minister I. C. Nollet January 8.
Mr. Nollet said 3,000 applications have been received from farmers who have qualified for payments under the federal provincial program. The applications were from 24 municipalities and local improvement districts in northern and eastern Saskatchewan and the first cheques went out Jar-uary 8.
The Liberals, typical of their understanding of the agricultural situation in the west, started out by telling us through the spokesmen for their party that they knew nothing, a fact which did not require underscoring from our point of view. Those hon. gentlemen who sit in the front benches on the Liberal side and who participated in the debate today spoke about everything and nothing. Of particular interest were the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East who stated that the farmers in the west should receive this assistance provided it was also given to the eastern farmers.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I never said that at all. I said that I recognized that this measure was necessary to assist the plight of the western farmer but I said that I also thought at the same time there were other farmers in other parts of Canada who were entitled to the benefits of such legislation. However, I did not say that if there was no extension to other groups of farmers at this time in this particular legislation I would, on that account, be opposed to it. I imposed no such condition and I am sure the hon. gentleman who is a very fair-minded member will readily admit that that is, of course, what I did say.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is exactly what I have been trying to say. What the hon. gentleman just said is typical of the attitude of the Liberal government in the past-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS

You did nothing for all of Canada.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
While telling us about the sugar beet situation in the east the hon. gentleman also indicated his support of the present resolution in the same breath, and attempted to create the impression that if the Liberal party were in office it would have provided this type of assistance. The attitude of the hon. gentleman which is so typical of his party somewhat reminds me of an epitaph on a tombstone:
Here lies the father of 29;
He'd have had more If he'd had time.
Hon. members of the Liberal party indicated that they lacked an understanding of the situation in western Canada. If they lacked that understanding they would have been unable to provide assistance to meet the general need that exists there.
I do not wish to digress from the main points it is my hope to raise at this time. I wish to point out to the committee why this legislation is necessary which may assist my Liberal friends in reaching the understanding they confess they lack.
Many of the reasons which were valid at the time when the cash advance legislation was introduced are valid in the present instance with respect to the present legislation. At the time of the introduction of the cash advance legislation the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as reported at page 351 of Hansard of October 24, 1957, stated:
The legislation is necessary because of the large surplus of wheat which has been accumulated in recent years due to a number of factors such as larger than average crops, a reduction in exports because of the loss of former markets, increased productivity per acre, subsidized competition from other wheat exporting countries, and so on.
It is ironical that in those days there was a great need because of abundance; today it is because of lack of grain that this legislation is necessary. Because my area is affected more than other areas I want to bring to the attention of the members of this committee a statement that was attributed to the wheat board reminding the farmers that they should not harvest their tough and damp grain. I say it is most unfortunate that that statement was made. Perhaps they should have reminded the farmers that they should not harvest their grain in a damp condition, but, as most farmers who have knowledge of the situation know, tough grain will keep perhaps for a long period of time. That statement should not have been made. The wheat board did not want any tough or damp grain. When they heard that statement many farmers having wet grain held back their harvesting. Elevator agents dissuaded the farmers from going into the field when the moisture content of the wheat was anywhere around
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

15 per cent. I am sure grain with that moisture content would have kept. Anyone who has any experience would have known that this type of grain would have kept.
I should like to read a quotation from the North Star of Norquay, dated Friday, November 27, 1959, just to indicate how serious the situation is, particularly in my area. The headline reads:
71. Sask. Municipalities Hit Hardest
The article goes on to say:
Seventy one Saskatchewan rural municipalities or local improvement districts contain 100 or more farms with at least 50 per cent of the crop still unharvested. A total of 30,233 farms were listed.
The tables were prepared by the statistics branch of the Saskatchewan department of agriculture and are the ones on which the bureau of statistics bases its summaries.
The article goes on to say:
The R.M. of Clayton tops the list in this area showing a total of 674 farms with 75 per cent and over unthreshed wheat.
In the list of municipalities having 50 to 74 per cent with unthreshed wheat, the R.M. of St. Philips is listed having 381 farms, R.M. of Keys 443 and R.M. of Livingston 537.
I think I have indicated the seriousness of the situation. There is another article in this paper entitled:
Farmers Meeting at Swan Plain
The article goes on to say:
A meeting of the Saskatchewan farmers' union was held at Swan Plain hall on November 19 with 44 members in attendance.
This telegram was forwarded to the Minister of Agriculture:
Disastrous conditions due to unharvested crops. Financial position of farmers desperate, urge immediate assistance.
I think this indicates why this type of legislation is necessary. The government is acting, as has been indicated by the Minister of Agriculture, to provide some form of assistance and has indicated what measures would be provided for relief. What the Minister of Agriculture did not mention was that the moving of hay and straw into areas where shortage existed on a 50-50 basis with each of the provinces was also to be undertaken.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: There is no legislation on that either.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
I want to point out that the federal government has given an undertaking whereby they would assist the provinces in payments to the individual farmers to the tune of $3 per acre to any individual farmer who had been prevented by snow conditions from harvesting 50 per cent or more of his crop. The hon. member for Assiniboia told us earlier that the government

Advance Payments to Grain Producers
merely wanted the farmer to incur another debt. I have before me application form H which is the one used by the Saskatchewan government in making the 1959-60 acreage payments on unharvested crops. The second item states:
That I normally depend on the income from my farm for my livelihood and that due to bad weather I have not been able to thresh 50 per cent of my crop acreage.
This particular item disqualified many school teachers, elevator operators, caterpillar operators, service station operators, small grocery store operators who also farm, and we have many of those in Saskatchewan. Incidentally, it also disqualified members of parliament. It also disqualified the landlords because someone who is renting land but is also occupied in some other form of endeavour cannot qualify. For the landlords that is a hardship. They cannot qualify for assistance. It is because of this that legislation such as this is being provided today and this present legislation is necessary. I think that the opposition members as well as-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee took recess at six o'clock I was just remarking that the landlord who has rented land to a tenant who has an occupation other than farming could not qualify for the acreage payment. This is one of the reasons why the legislation preceded by this resolution we have before us today is necessary. Perhaps another reason that could be advanced could be illustrated by the clause which the provincial government of Saskatchewan has inserted. I must say that I am somewhat disappointed in this clause which requires a person to state he normally depends on income from the farm for his livelihood and that, due to bad weather, he has been unable to thresh 50 per cent of his crop acreage. These are the people who, for years, have advocated a change in the P.F.A.A., and I am glad to state that the present government introduced these changes. It is disappointing that Saskatchewan should insert a clause which would disqualify the very same people that they have been attempting to qualify under P.F.A.A., namely those who are gainfully employed in other occupations or who have been taking up other occupations to supplement their income.
I think that another point that should be advanced here is a point that one of the elevator agents made to me during my travels around the constituency. He mentioned that there is a possibility of a farmer in great need of assistance but who may have some grain that could later have been used for seed. This farmer could request a cash advance from the elevator agent and later find that he might have used this grain for seed. He would then be in a position where he would be almost perjuring himself. This is one of the reasons for giving the proposed legislation careful scrutiny and approval because we should not allow a situation which may cause a farmer to perjure himself. I mention that only as a possibility because I do not think you will find too many such cases.
I do not want to continue much longer, but there are a few questions to which I should like answers. Should losses be incurred after advances have been taken, either in the form of loans or cash advances, how long will the government permit for the repayment of these advances? I know that in my area particularly there is the danger of deer and elk roaming the field and mice and other rodents often invade the stooked fields. I should like to know whether the government will permit these farmers who, perhaps through no fault of their own, find themselves unable to harvest another crop next year, to extend the period for repayment.
In conclusion I would give a bit of friendly advice to the Liberal opposition by suggesting that if they do not know the subject they can always talk about the weather, and this time they certainly would be right.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS

One which would help is the re-appraisal of the wheat board policy with regard to shipments to the lakehead which incidentally has also affected the employees on the railways.
With regard to the help for farmers which this resolution before us is supposed to provide, we were taken by surprise, to put it mildly, when we discovered that it contains an entirely different proposal from that which was made to the provinces last November as reported in the press. Prairie farmers who have been unable to harvest because of bad weather-that was a proposal which we read about in the paper-were to receive up to $600 as a sort of special assistance. Actually, under this scheme the government intended to pay only $300, and that only if the government of the province concerned contributed an equal amount. In reality, the government has placed the provincial governments in a very embarrassing position.

There is also another condition, that to be eligible for this particular assistance a farmer must have harvested less than 50 per cent of his crop. Someone has referred to this condition as being callous and arbitrary, because if a farmer had harvested 55 per cent of his crop he would not share in the benefits, whereas his neighbour who had harvested, say, 40 per cent of his crop would be eligible for assistance. I would suggest that if assistance is contemplated the fairest method would be to treat everyone alike on a pro rata basis. However, this bill deals only with loans guaranteed by the government, with no specified rate of interest, incidentally.
I think that is an objection. There should be a specified rate of interest, in these circumstances which we are discussing, in any proposal which the government is advancing. We are not opposed to this relief which will be given to our western farmers. Every speaker so far on this side of the house has made it very clear that we are supporting this resolution.
Mr. Chairman, it is my duty to bring to the attention of this house the fact that there are farmers in my constituency who would welcome the availability of a loan guaranteed by the government. I would say that this provision should be made available, in the event of necessity arising in any community affecting the farmers, to all the farmers on an equal basis. As I say, Mr. Chairman, we are in favour of this legislation but I would express my sincere hope that similar legislation would cover all farmers in every part of Canada, wherever a similar need should arise.
I do not wish to take any more time, because I think every hon. member is very much concerned about the question. I do not represent a particularly large farming community, but there are some farmers in my constituency, as there are in nearly all constituencies, except, perhaps, the metropolitan areas of the cities. I would like to read in conclusion a letter which appeared in the Family Herald of Medora, Manitoba, which is as follows:
The October snowstorms of 1959 are the worst disaster that has ever hit farmers in Manitoba. There is a universal shortage of winter feed and bedding for livestock. There is no source of additional supplies of either hay or straw. Surplus hay has been bought up. The farmers without cash to buy hay must sacrifice their breeding stock.
I might say that that is exactly what is happening in my constituency. In the district of Thunder Bay the crop of hay was damaged last season, with the result that farmers have not been able to keep their livestock going to the same degree and extent they have in the past. There is need for assistance too. The letter continues:


Already many have done this at heavy financial loss.
P.F.A.A. survey of poor crop townships was made as usual. Why was not the P.F.A.A. survey used at the same time to estimate the farmers' losses? Why can not the P.F.A.A. be used to make relief payments? We need cash-not empty promises of long term credit, loans and future crop insurance.
This, Mr. Chairman, is merely an indication of what is happening, not only in Manitoba but all over the country. For that reason I say that the government should bring forward some legislation which will cover all farmers in every constituency of Canada.

Yes, I am aware of that situation, Mr. Chairman. Furthermore, I am aware of the fact that there are millions of bushels of damp grain in western Canada today for which that space will be required when it is finally dried by the drying capacity of those terminals across the country.
Almost every hon. member on the opposition side has said today that he is not opposed to this legislation. All I want to say on that is this: Thou doth protest too loudly. If we go back to the debates in the House of Commons to an occasion similar to today, when those in the official opposition had the opportunity to bring in legislation somewhat

similar to the legislation in contemplation now, we will find where the members of the Liberal party stood at that time.
The hon. member for Assiniboia had some things to say upon which I would like to refresh his memory. He was particularly worried about those farmers in the province of Saskatchewan who were not going to get payment in time and who were going to suffer because of the actions of the federal government. The hon. member for Assiniboia should know better than to try to leave that misunderstanding to the country. He should try to tell that to the people in the province of Saskatchewan. I would like to draw his attention, first of all, to the statement made by the minister of agriculture in Saskatchewan on January 16-following on the remarks made by the hon. member for Mackenzie-which were as follows:
Farm relief payments in Saskatchewan are averaging $2.75 an acre, agriculture minister Nollet said Friday.
By Thursday night the government had approved payment of 6,800 applications covering 776,000 acres and involving $2,114,000.
At the end of the week it had close to 3,000 applications on hand that had not been processed.
About 3,000 cheques have been mailed to applicants.
This appeared in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix on January 16, 1960. The hon. member for Mackenzie pointed out that there were some 32,000 farmers in the province of Saskatchewan who needed help. I say to you in the House of Commons today that the people of Saskatchewan know who was responsible for the regulations which ruled out the possibility of so many receiving assistance in respect of their loss and hardship. And there were those who said that there have been delays. I think it was the hon. member for Assiniboia who said that there were delays in bringing aid to the farm people. When hon. members talk of delays let them remember that the premier of Saskatchewan, the Hon. T. C. Douglas, chose the period of greatest anxiety to leave his province in order to sun himself in the Mediterranean area.
Much has been said today about an affront to parliament. The hon. member for Essex East mentioned the responsibility of parliament, and I think he also used the words "abuse", "rights" and "privileges". He then went on to exhibit his true regard for the western Canadian farmers and the people of western Canada. He referred with sarcasm to the Prime Minister going out to western Canada to the meeting at Winnipeg. His colleague, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, was more friendly toward the western farmer.

During the past two days I have been refreshing my memory with regard to a certain famous debate which took place in the House of Commons on January 27, 1956, but before I go on to that let me recall that the hon. member for Assiniboia mentioned that the provincial governments were providing assistance for moving fodder. What the hon. member did not mention was that the federal government was sharing in the cost of moving that fodder.
With the introduction of this measure all members of the committee, those who sit in the opposition and those who sit with the government, have before them a vivid reminder of other days, those days in parliament when a party with an overwhelming majority cracked the whip so unmercifully in regard to its own private members that it even became dangerous for one of their distinguished colleagues to appear on television in this country. I refer to my distinguished predecessor, the former Liberal member for Rosthern, who felt the whip hand of a conforming demand by the cabinet. He was a good friend of the hon. member for Essex East, but notwithstanding that connection he came into the house on January 27, 1956 to take a stand which was, to say the least, not in conformity with the opinion he had expressed to his electors or to the press in western Canada or with his electors' opinions as expressed in a famous telegram sent by the former hon. member to his chieftain, the then prime minister of this country, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, and the minister of trade and commerce of those days, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe.
The measure now before us is complementary to the legislation which formed one of the first acts of a Conservative government. It reminds the people of my constituency of the valley of humiliation through which their member of those other days trod. We cannot ever think he did it voluntarily. And yet all Liberal-minded people in my constituency- and I say that word with a capital "L"-will never quite forgive the surrender of those rights and privileges enjoyed by an ordinary member of the House of Commons which ultimately led to the entire Liberal party wallowing in that same valley of humiliation which became epitomized in the pipe lines debate some months later. Oh, and how they upheld the supremacy of parliament and the rights of the private members, and the opposition with its rights. And Howe, the minister of trade and commerce, sat where the Minister of Trade and Commerce sits today.
I ask hon. members to turn back the pages of Hansard to the statement read by the Minister of Finance before the recess-page

It seems to me that there should not be a prolonged debate on this legislation. The provisions of the bill have been in effect since November 15.
Not satisfied with controlling his own supporters, he was trying to control the opposition as well. There was the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate; there was the hon. member for Essex East, the discoverer of abuse, affront and lack of privilege; and there was the rest of that unhappy group.
This legislation has been asked for by farmers and farm organizations. I know it is needed and that it will be helpful in assisting many people in western Canada, but I welcome it on another ground as well, and that is that it is a reminder to us all, wherever we sit in this House of Commons, of the comparative freedom from coercion which is necessary if a private member is to be enabled to do his job effectively and, likewise, if those who serve in senior positions are to be spared the humiliation that is the sure reward of those who might thus encouraged take on a "Howe" complex. The Prime Minister is to be commended for his action in calling the Winnipeg meeting of farm people in December which focussed attention on the plight of all those who had suffered such severe affliction, and I ask all members of the committee to support this measure.

provisional payments to the producers for the crop year 1959-1960, in respect of unthreshed grain in the designated area.
Of course, we readily support the legislation, but we regret one thing, i.e. that the resolution does not apply to the whole country.
Those who have been the victims of a disaster have our sympathy because in eastern Canada we have been through similar conditions and shall probably experience them again in the future. Often, perhaps, unfortunately too often, our eastern farmers suffer damage either from wind storms, hail or other weather conditions impossible to prevent.
I recall that, last year, when we were dealing with a bill on the farm loan, I mentioned this lack to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness).
I am convinced that, if I take the matter up again, he will tell me that we were dealing at the time with crop insurance. He is, however, the same man who, in 1958, stated before the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that in the province of Quebec, a crop insurance plan would run into snags. I wonder why this government has not extended the bill so as to cover all provinces in Canada.
If we gladly support the legislation with regard to the western farmers, we, in the east, would like to benefit from it too.
Mr. Chairman, I have been deeply annoyed and even shocked by the interjections which the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) made this afternoon. He mentioned, among other things, that we in the eastern part of the country, were jealous. I may assure you, Mr. Chairman, that there can be no question of jealousy, for we support this resolution. the country, did not consider it proper to modify this resolution in such a way as to cover farmers in eastern Canada.

Mr. Chairman, this is my first opportunity to address you as chairman of this committee of the whole. I should like to add my words of congratulation to those you have already heard on your appointment to this very important position.
We have had a surprising amount of politics injected into the debate today. I do not propose to add to those political expressions. In certain areas of the west the emergency is extremely serious and the people there will not take lightly the way some hon. members in this debate have treated the measure embodied in the resolution before us.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is anxious to get the important bill foreshadowed by the resolution before us piloted through the house as quickly as possible. We on the government side are just as concerned to bring into effect the act to provide cash advances on unthreshed grain, the wheat, oats and barley crops that are now lying under the snow on prairie farms through no fault of the farm operators. I therefore intend to speak only briefly tonight.
As a member from the prairies representing a constituency comprised of urban and rural residents in almost equal proportion, I wish to congratulate the minister and the government on the quick action taken in bringing in this proposed bill, together with another proposed bill providing for guaranteed bank loans to farmers who still have their grain unthreshed. I am sure it will be noted by both farmers and business men on the prairies that the government took action as soon as possible after the opening of parliament to bring into effect what this proposed bill is intended to regarding snow-covered grain, something in addition to direct payments, payments of up to $600 per farmer to those adversely affected by the unseasonal weather last fall.
The bill envisaged by this resolution and the other legislation, concerning which notice
Advance Payments to Grain Producers has been given by the Minister of Finance relating to extra financial assistance in meeting the problem of unthreshed grain are the first measures that will come before us this session. The throne speech debate has been postponed in order to put the legislation through. I wish to draw this to the attention of the prairie provinces and to emphasize the fact that this government is watching the western farm situation very closely and is prepared to act quickly when an emergency situation arises.
My own constituency of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre was not too greatly affected by the adverse harvest weather. Most of the farmers in my area have their crops harvested and can obtain cash advances on their farm-stored grain under the plan brought in by this government-I wish to emphasize that it was brought in by this government-in 1957. Any calamity that hits one section of the west as the early autumn rain and snow hit the northern areas is the common problem of all farming areas and all who are engaged in the agricultural industry welcome the action of this government.
As a farm operator myself I recall a similar snow and rain catastrophe which struck one autumn a few years ago and to which reference has already been made in this debate. My own crop and those of many other farmers was under snow all winter. On that occasion there was no assistance available from the Liberal government of that day. There was not even a suggestion from the Liberal government that there would be cash advances on grain under the snow such as has been proposed by this government. Fortunately, the following spring, following the year I referred to in which we had the crop loss before, was an exceptionally dry one and we were able to salvage much of the crop. We did that without direct financial help from the Liberal government. We hope that this coming spring will be such that the farmers will also be able to salvage the crops still unthreshed. If it turns out to be a wet spring it may not be possible to recover enough grain to fully repay from crop proceeds the cash advances given under this bill. It is because of this possibility that I have risen to speak tonight for this short time.
On July 22, 1958, the Minister of Trade and Commerce brought in an amendment to the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act of 1957 to provide for the consolidation of cash advances from one crop year to another. In other words, any amount owing on the cash advanced at the end of the crop year could be carried over as an advance to the next

The third major amendment provides for the consolidation of cash advances from one crop year to the other. This will make it possible for a producer who has not fully repaid his cash advance through no fault of his own, which means because his quota has not been large enough to permit him to deliver or because there has been some difficulty for which he is not responsible, to obtain a further cash advance on his new crop year if desired. The two advances would then be consolidated and recorded in the permit book, and as quotas were raised the producer would repay both advances.
I hope that at later stages the Minister of Trade and Commerce will at least make this point clear and thus answer some of the main questions that have been asked me regarding this measure.
Again I want to congratulate the minister and the government on bringing in this proposed measure so quickly.

The second misconception seems to be that this money is coming out of the federal treasury. This is a measure to provide cash advances against the delivery of certain grain which, at the moment, is under the snow. It is expected that the farmers may thresh at least part of this grain and when it is delivered they will repay the cash advance. The main reason that this legislation can be brought forward is the fact that prairie grain producers have decided they want to market their grain through a government board. They support the government board. This is, in part, a measure that has been brought about because there is a public body, namely the Canadian wheat board, handling the marketing, assembling and the grading of grain.
If the farmers in other parts of Canada wish the same kind of general advantages that flow


from marketing their products through a central selling agency, then they would need to ask for the appropriate legislation to enable them to do so. Then if they should get into a disaster this kind of legislation might be brought forward by the government. The only charge on the treasury so far as this legislation is concerned is the cost of administration and the cost of interest on the cash advances for a very short period.
We have had a rather wide ranging discussion, Mr. Chairman, of the general grain situation on the prairies brought about by this emergency, and the various steps that have been taken to deal with it. There is, of course, one important step which the government has not taken. I asked the minister earlier-and I hope he will reply to my question-whether or not the government had considered the possibility of paying deficiency payments on grain that has already been marketed. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce will readily realize and as the Minister of Finance I am certain realizes, such a step would put much more money into the pockets of needy grain producers than will the legislation that is being brought forward. I think that this emergency, at least in a substantial degree, could have been met, along with other measures, by providing deficiency payments on western grain.
I am wondering whether the minister can give the committee any idea at all of what estimate there is as to the use that will be made of this legislation. I think the government must have at least some general idea of how much it is in demand and of what use can be made of it. When we had a debate a couple of years ago about general cash advance legislation I believe at that time it was the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources who estimated that there might be as much as $150 million or even a larger sum made available under that legislation. I am quoting from memory but I think my memory is probably accurate when I say that about $33 million or $35 million in cash advances was made available the first year. In other words, even though western grain producers under that measure had access to an interest free advance they did not rush in to get that advance since a relatively small proportion of the farmers who could obtain the advance availed themselves of the legislation.
In view of the amount of grain that is under the snow and in view of the bill that will be forthcoming as a result of the passage of this resolution, I am wondering whether the minister has made some estimate as to the use that is likely to be made of this

I might answer that question in this way. I have not made any attempt to forecast the number of applicants for these provisional payments that we are proposing. However, looking at the situation with regard to the cash advances under the earlier legislation we find that in the first year of the operation of that act 50,412 farmers made application. The total amount of money involved was $35,203,467. In the second crop year of the operation of the cash advance legislation, 45,341 farmers made application. The total amount of money that was advanced was $34,369,653. In the present crop year, five months of which have now gone by, 45,076 applications have been received for cash advances, for a total of $35,545,444.
The areas that are affected in the northern parts of the three prairie provinces, when the estimate of damage was made in the middle of October, amounted to 25 per cent of the general crop. Subsequently that figure has been reduced because of the remarkable effort at harvesting grain during the months of November and December, and the number of applicants for assistance under this proposed bill may not be very great. I would hesitate to make an estimate as to whether it would be say another 10,000 people who would make application or whether it would be only half that number or as to whether the amount of money involved would be one eighth of what has already been applied for under the cash advance legislation.
Nevertheless, whether the number of applicants is large or small or whether the amount of money is large or small this legislation will meet the requirements of individuals who are having difficulty in obtaining cash this year, particularly those who are in the awkward position of not being able to harvest any of their crop. I think we shall find that a great many farmers have harvested some of their crop and on that harvested grain may perhaps already have received a cash advance under the other legislation. This proves I was right in the suggestion I made, and we might be much further ahead if we had not wandered astray as the hon. member for Assiniboia has wandered astray in the course of his remarks today. My admiration for the hon. member as a debater is sometimes diminished by the fact that he diverges from the subject under discussion which, in this instance, is the question of provisional payments for farmers who have not been able to harvest their crops. Yet the hon. member talks about all manner of other things, knowing well, from his long experience in this house, that he is completely out of order. He seized the opportunity to smuggle in a request for a statement of government policy, a request which was answered by the Prime Minister this afternoon. I wonder that a person occupying the responsible position which the hon. member does in the party he represents cannot follow more closely the example which was set him by his eminent predecessors.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: I do not want to instruct you in your duties, Mr. Chairman. I am quite prepared to go ahead and answer the statement made by the minister, but I do not want to elbow anyone else out if you care to give him the floor. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said I was trying to smuggle something in-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: If the hon. member has completed his speech, I was going to recognize the hon. member for Acadia.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
First of all, I would like to congratulate you, Mr. Chairman, on your appointment to the office you now hold and wish you every success in your difficult task. As my name has been mentioned frequently in this discussion it appears to me that I should say a few words.
It seems to me that a great deal of the criticism which has been directed against this bill has been brought about by a lack of understanding of the conditions in western Canada this fall. I do not think any of the old timers in the west can recall a similar autumn, or one that even compared with it as far as the disaster effect is concerned. I have spoken to a great many of the old timers in my constituency and they all tell me they have never seen anything like it.

Advance Payments to Grain Producers
As the hon. member for Meadow Lake said, there was a record amount of rainfall in the first part of the harvest season and then 20 inches of snow. Similar conditions occurred in my own constituency, particularly in the western half which had as much as six inches of rain in the last two weeks of August and then rain on about every second day during September. The fields were so wet that in many cases farmers could not get in with a tractor even to swath. I want the committee to realize that these conditions, which amounted to disaster, were brought about by the weather and that no fault at all could be attached to the farmers.
This government is prepared to take action with respect to the five measures that have been mentioned but we will proceed with one measure at a time. They will certainly be welcome in the west and will be of much benefit. It appears to be the general belief of hon. members of the opposition that these measures will benefit every farmer in western Canada. We would like to see that, of course, but let me inform the committee that these five measures will not have that effect. I hope they will benefit those who need assistance most but certainly they will not represent a blanket benefit applying to every western farmer. I hope that is clearly understood.
The hon. member for Assiniboia spoke about deficiency payments. One could speak all night on that subject. I fail to see how a farmer with his crop under snow could benefit by getting an additional sum per bushel for the crop when he cannot harvest it until spring depending on weather conditions at that time.
The hon. member for Essex East said that this government should not have gone ahead with the measure until it had come to parliament with it. To do so would mean a delay of two or three months before the farmers would receive any benefit at all. Some are already receiving payments as was pointed out today due to the speedy action with which the government met this emergency.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River stated that he was surprised about all this. Certainly he should be surprised. His party while in office thought it was not possible to bring in cash advances. It was considered impossible by the Liberals. Resolution number 6 on today's order paper provides for the making of provisional payments to producers in respect of unthreshed grain, which is along the line of cash advances. Some hon. gentlemen appear to be of the view that this measure is one of the smallest of the five that have been mentioned but I believe it will benefit a greater number of farmers than
most of the other measures because no matter whether a farmer has 10 per cent or 90 per cent of his grain unthreshed it will still be possible for him to receive some benefit through the legislation foreshadowed by this resolution.
Those are a few of the points that I feel have not been sufficiently clarified in this debate. Another thing which should be pointed out is that Alberta has probably suffered to a greater extent than the other prairie provinces. That was borne out in the statistics released by the wheat pools throughout the fall. They indicated there were more bushels unharvested in Alberta than in the other prairie provinces. Alberta is a mixed farming area. An extension of cash advance payments will benefit mixed farmers assisting them to stay in business and maintain operations with respect to their other endeavours.
Much mention was made today about grain storage. I was pleased to hear there is storage on the west coast and the ports on lake Superior. As was pointed out, we will probably need this storage before the spring harvest. Much of the wheat is harvested damp. We should all thank the wheat board for extending permits to those farmers with damp grain. At this time in many cases farmers with damp grain deliver up to a 6-bushel quota on their crops. This is a good measure. The wheat board will endeavour to fill the storage as soon as possible due to these measures we have discussed today.
I do not wish to leave the impression that I am creating a rift between the east and west when I say that there appears to be some jealousy with respect to these payments. This is a disaster payment. In establishing it this government has created a splendid precedent. Certainly if a disaster occurred in central Canada or in the mari-times similar assistance should be considered. I believe that point was overlooked to start with and I hope my remarks will be of some assistance in clearing it up.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
In listening to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Chairman, I was further disturbed by the position he has taken when he stated that he felt if the bill was not controversial it would not need to be preceded by the resolution stage of debate. Then again, he said this particular resolution is not controversial. I do not know what would happen if we were discussing something which was controversial because there has been a great deal of controversy in this debate today although everyone here is in support of the motion. I would point out to the minister that if parliament is not given the opportunity to have a general debate on the resolution stage it would be impossible

speechtext: Has there been any suggestion made to the effect that there should not be a debate on the resolution stage?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. I was referring to remarks the minister used to make when he was in opposition. He said that was not the position he took.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: On the contrary, Mr. Chairman, I did not say that. At no time did I say that. Let me point out that I was on the rules committee in 1954-55. At that time the suggestion was made that this stage in the debating procedure should be omitted. I opposed that and would continue to oppose it if such a suggestion were made today. I think that stage of our procedure should be maintained.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
I am glad to have that clarification, Mr. Chairman, and I believe it was necessary. I am glad to see the minister taking that position and certainly I agree with him that this stage in our procedure should be maintained.
I do not think, nor did the Chairman, that I was violating the rules in asking questions about what factors the government had considered in bringing forward this resolution. I believe it is very much in order to ask the government whether or not it had considered the question of making deficiency payments which, by themselves, would put a great deal of money into the hands of the very producers who have grain under the snow.
The hon. member for Acadia wondered how that would help farmers who have not threshed their grain. The request was that deficiency payments should be made on grain that had been marketed in previous years. If that were done it would put money into the hands of the vast majority of farmers who are now adversely affected by weather conditions. The only farmer who could not be helped by such a measure would be one who was a young person and who started farming this past year. Deficiency payments would be a decided asset to western Canada. I am certain that the government will hear more during the session on this point and will receive many more delegations and submissions on the point until it gives a satisfactory reply.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as so many have said tonight, it was not my intention to enter this debate. This particular problem does not affect my area. Sunny southern Alberta is just her usual sunny self. We have had a good year. With respect to the discussion that has occurred concerning farm income, let me say I am fully confident that our particular locality will enjoy an income for 1959 equal to that of 1958 when the computations have been made.
I am constrained to say that if all the heat that has been generated in this chamber this afternoon and evening could be wafted over our western prairies the need for this legislation would have evaporated. We are all agreed on this proposed legislation and yet we go on talking about it. It is my hope that we may soon come to a unanimous decision with respect to it and proceed to other business.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this late stage these will be my last remarks if the minister will answer a question or two which I raised earlier and which I think are pertinent to the discussion that we have had. I am sure the minister will admit that part of the purpose of our procedure is to obtain certain information which will be helpful in debate at the next stage, which is the second reading of the bill.
We learn by the grapevine that the Prime Minister is anxious to proceed tomorrow with the speech from the throne and we will not be dealing with this legislation. Consequently, I urge the government to have a look at the desirability of bringing in legislation that would encompass the proposition that was outlined by the Prime Minister to the provinces. It seems to me that the limits of his proposition could easily be put in legislative form, and I am sure that not only members in this group but members in the government party would like the opportunity of discussing this with the government in a proper form and at this time when we are considering the plight of the western farmer who has unthreshed grain.
The essence of the resolution is that it is expedient to do something for the farmer with unthreshed grain. In that connection the Prime Minister indicated at the beginning that P.F.A.A. payments would be accelerated. We have heard nothing further from the ministers since I have advanced that reminder. In addition to this, we find considerable confusion and lack of information from the ministry with respect to the extent of helping the western farmer through the agencies or schemes of the provincial governments, and the degree of acceptance by them of the proposition that was made to them for outright

Advance Payments to Grain Producers
grants to the farmers in the most necessitous conditions, provided that they had more than 50 per cent of their crops unthreshed.
The Minister of Agriculture admitted that he was not fully up to date as to what has taken place in the matter of distribution of funds in the pockets of those helped under the proposition. We have had some help from the personal knowledge of some of the hon. members such as the hon. member for Mackenzie, the hon. member for Rosthern and others who have indicated that at least in the province of Saskatchewan some action has taken place. I indicated that, according to the press, in the province of the Minister of Trade and Commerce there apparently was some considerable delay. The minister may know something about it, but the Minister of Agriculture seemingly did not. In a press report dated January 7, 1960, we find the following:
Hon. George Hutton, minister of agriculture, has announced January 23 as the deadline for receipt of application forms for the assistance.
Therefore, presumably, there is something lacking there comparable to what has been announced by members from Saskatchewan as taking place there. When we are considering the plight of the western farmers we should have information to the fullest possible extent as to what some of these other supplementary forms of assistance have been right up to date.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ADVANCE PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Before the minister replies, as I am sure he intends to do, to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, I should like to join in the plea that he has made to the ministry because I recognize that it is not for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to decide this. It is perhaps more for the Minister of Finance to decide and for the ministry to reconsider the attitude of ignoring parliament which they have taken with respect to the most important of the three aspects of this matter, and to bring in legislation. The reason I am prompted to intervene again is that the Minister of Finance, speaking just after I did before dinner, referred to what Mr. Howe had done in 1956, and that is precisely what we are asking the government to do now.
What the government did in 1956 was to tell the banks that they would ask parliament to pass legislation to underwrite those loans, and when the session was called this was in the speech from the throne, and legislation was introduced at the earliest possible moment. What we are asking the ministry to do now is to show the same respect for parliament that Mr. Howe did in 1956, instead of by-passing parliament, ignoring it altogether, and allowing the provinces to go ahead and spend the money and then come in months
later and ask us to behave like a lot of rubber stamps. The ministry have got a reprieve of 24 hours, and I appeal to them to remember those speeches made by the Prime Minister about parliament and to remember that the first function of parliament is to control the expenditure of the people's money, and to bring the legislation here and let us deal with it and let us deal with it on Thursday.

The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Has the federal government received representations from any municipal body or city council, requesting the federal government to include a no discrimination provision in all National Housing Act transactions and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans, to prevent discrimination against persons because of race, colour or creed?
2.	If so, from whom were such representations received, and what reply was made to the representations?
Answer by: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of
Public Works):
1.	Yes.
2.	The Windsor city council.
The reply given was as follows:
Ottawa, December 16, 1959 Mr. J. B. Adamac,
Office of the Clerk, City Hall,
Windsor, Ontario.
Mr. J. B. Adamac,
The Prime Minister has asked me to reply to the resolution adopted by the Windsor council at its meeting held on November 9, 1959.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which is the federal agency responsible for the administration of the National Housing Act, subscribes fully to non-discrimination in all its transactions.
The corporation includes in its construction contracts a clause providing that the contractor shall not refuse employment to anyone on the grounds of race, national origin, colour or religion.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in insuring loans made by lending institutions under part I of the National Housing Act, or making direct loans available, does not discriminate. It is primarily concerned with the ability of purchasers to meet their mortgage payments.
The corporation in approving purchasers who may buy houses from builders does not discriminate either for or against any race, group or class. The relationship between the corporation and the builder or home owner is that of lender and borrower. As the corporation is not a party to transactions between builders and purchasers it does not
Question
exercise control over the terms and conditions of sale which might be prescribed by a builder. Any attempts to take such action by the corporation, might be construed as violating normal property and civil rights; the corporation would be placed in the position of attempting to dictate the conditions by which a builder may sell his housing units.
I might mention that limited dividend projects built under the National Housing Act are for rental to families of low income and that is the only relevant restriction applicable to such projects. The corporation does not make limited dividend loans to sponsors who desire to rent exclusively to members of one particular group. The only restrictions on tenant selection of such projects are those governing family income and sometimes age.
As you know, federal-provincial projects are managed by local housing authorities appointed by the partnership in consultation with the municipalities. From time to time the corporation has had discussions with the province of Ontario in which the majority of these projects are located regarding their management and directions have periodically been given to the effect that no discrimination on the grounds of race, colour, creed or national origin to be exercised in the tenant selection thereof. The housing authorities have recently confirmed that they do not discriminate in selecting tenants.
I should perhaps mention that in slum clearance projects where a low rental project is to be built, the corporation inserts a condition in the contract that all persons displaced from the slum clearance area are to have the opportunity to be relocated in the rental project. In fact, there are a number of coloured persons residing in federal provincial projects, one of whom was the first chairman of the tenants association in Lawrence Heights.
There is of course, no discrimination in the selection of tenants in corporation-owned projects.
The government is in full accord with the principles of non-discrimination and you may be assured that your representations have our earnest and sympathetic consideration. Legislation covering non-discrimination affecting property and civil rights would not appear to come within the provisions of the National Housing Act.
Yours very truly, David J. Walker.
